name: The Gut-Brain Axis
what: This subtopic introduces the gut and gut microbiota, defines the gut-brain axis as a bidirectional connection between the gut and the brain via the enteric and central nervous systems, and examines emerging research linking gut microbiota composition to stress, mental illness, and behaviour.
why: The gut-brain axis is an explicitly listed area of emerging research in the study design. Students must understand the mechanism of bidirectional communication, the role of gut microbiota, and the nature and limitations of the evidence — including why definitive causal claims cannot yet be made.

items.title: I can define the gut and distinguish between gut microbiota and the gut microbiome
items.what: The gut (gastrointestinal tract) is the tube from mouth to anus responsible for digestion. Gut microbiota refers to all the microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, viruses) that live in the gut. The gut microbiome refers to all the genes of those microorganisms. A diverse microbiota with more 'good' bacteria is associated with better gut health.
items.why: These terms are distinct and both appear in exam questions. Confusing microbiota with microbiome is a common error. Understanding what constitutes a healthy microbiota is the foundation for understanding how gut health relates to psychological processes.
items.example: If a student's gut has many different species of beneficial bacteria (diverse microbiota), this is associated with better overall health outcomes, including lower levels of stress.

items.title: I can define the gut-brain axis and explain what makes it bidirectional
items.what: The gut-brain axis is the bidirectional connection between the gut and the brain through the enteric nervous system and the central nervous system. Bidirectional means communication flows both ways: the gut influences the brain and the brain influences the gut. The vagus nerve is the primary physical pathway for this communication, with approximately 80-90% of its fibres carrying signals from gut to brain.
items.why: The bidirectional nature of the relationship is central to understanding how stress affects the gut and how gut health affects stress. Exam questions may ask students to explain or give examples of communication in both directions.
items.example: When a student feels anxious before an exam (brain to gut), they may experience stomach cramps. Conversely, a student with irritable bowel syndrome (gut to brain) may experience heightened anxiety as a result.

items.title: I can describe the role of the enteric nervous system in the gut-brain axis
items.what: The enteric nervous system is the network of nerves in the gut and is a subdivision of the autonomic nervous system. It communicates with the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), allowing gut-related conditions to influence brain function and brain-related conditions to influence gut function.
items.why: Students must be able to correctly locate the enteric nervous system within the broader nervous system hierarchy and explain its role in the gut-brain relationship, as this is likely to be assessed directly.
items.example: A person with inflammatory bowel disease (a gut condition) has altered enteric nervous system signals being sent to the brain, which can contribute to symptoms of anxiety or depression.

items.title: I can describe emerging research evidence for the gut-brain axis, including germ-free animal studies and microbiota composition research
items.what: Germ-free animal studies remove gut microorganisms from animals and compare their behaviour to conventional animals. Findings include increased anxiety-like behaviour, poorer memory, increased stress hormones, and less social interaction in germ-free mice. Human studies compare microbiota composition in people with and without mental health conditions and suggest links between gut microbiota and stress, depression, anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, and cognitive decline.
items.why: The study design specifically requires reference to emerging research. Students must be able to describe findings without overstating them as proven causal relationships, which reflects appropriate scientific literacy.
items.example: In one study, germ-free mice implanted with gut microbiota from humans with major depressive disorder began exhibiting depressive-like behaviours, suggesting a possible link between gut microbiota composition and mood.

items.title: I can explain the relationship between gut microbiota and stress, using the bidirectional nature of the gut-brain axis
items.what: The relationship between gut microbiota and stress is bidirectional. Experiencing stress can negatively affect the diversity and composition of gut microbiota. Conversely, having an unhealthy gut microbiota is linked to higher stress levels. This explains phenomena such as experiencing stomach discomfort when stressed and experiencing stress when suffering digestive problems.
items.why: This bidirectional relationship directly links gut-brain axis content to the broader topic of stress. Exam questions may present a scenario involving stress and gut symptoms and ask students to explain the connection.
items.example: A student who is chronically stressed about exams develops digestive discomfort (stress affecting the gut). Separately, a student with a gut condition may find their anxiety worsens when their gut symptoms flare (gut affecting stress levels).

items.title: I can explain why definitive conclusions about the gut-brain axis cannot yet be drawn
items.what: Because the gut-brain axis is an emerging area of research, findings are still evolving and sometimes contradictory. It is incorrect to state that gut microbiota causes stress or mental illness; rather, emerging research suggests possible connections. Animal studies are difficult to generalise to humans, and some studies using different strains of animals have produced conflicting results.
items.why: Scientific literacy requires understanding the difference between correlation and causation and between emerging findings and established consensus. This is explicitly acknowledged in the curriculum content and reflects the nature of this research area.
items.example: One study found less social engagement in germ-free mice; another study using a different strain of mice found normal social engagement. This contradiction shows the field is still developing and definitive conclusions are premature.
